17296507.extract:
# Ring of Nestor

## Introduction

The Ring of Nestor is a gold signet ring attributed to the Aegean Bronze Age and notable for its elaborate engraved imagery and its contested role within Minoan and Mycenaean religious and artistic traditions. Modern scholarship has focused on the ring’s complex iconography, its proposed Late Minoan dating, and ongoing debates about its authenticity and archaeological provenance. 

## Discovery, Dating, and Physical Description

Arthur Evans’s 1925 study describes a gold signet ring he termed the "Ring of Nestor" as part of what he called a "veritable royal treasure of gold signet-rings and bead-seals" from a Mycenaean rock-cut tomb near Thisbë in Boeotia. Evans presents the ring as one of several finely made gold signet rings, associating the assemblage with high-status or royal burial and emphasizing the exceptional wealth represented by the treasure. 

In Evans’s reconstruction, the tomb group and its grave goods are dated to the late Mycenaean period, correlated with the Cretan Late Minoan III timeframe. He situates the sepulchral treasure, including the Ring of Nestor, within this late phase of the Bronze Age, drawing on associated weapons, glass, and ceramic finds to support the chronological placement. 

A later online encyclopedia entry reports a different discovery context, stating that the Ring of Nestor is a gold signet ring discovered before 1907 at Kakovatos in Messenia, Greece. The same entry identifies the present location of the ring as the Ashmolean Museum at the University of Oxford, under inventory number AN1938.1130 and catalogued in the Corpus der Minoischen und Mykenischen Siegel as CMS VI.229. It notes that Evans donated the ring to the Ashmolean Museum in 1939. 

The online encyclopedia’s information box lists the ring’s material simply as gold and provides dimensions and weight, emphasizing that it is a large gold signet ring. While these measurements are presented as part of basic object data, they are reported without detailed discussion of manufacturing techniques in the summarized sources and thus have not been independently contextualized in the available scholarship cited here. 

The same online encyclopedia places the Ring of Nestor in the Late Minoan I period, approximately 1700–1450 BCE, and assigns it to Minoan culture, explicitly noting that this cultural attribution is disputed. By contrast, Evans’s original publication dates the sepulchral treasure, including the ring, to a late Mycenaean horizon corresponding to Late Minoan III, underlining a chronological shift between the early interpretation and later summaries. 

Theodore Eliopoulos’s 2013 article treats the Ring of Nestor as an object proposed to be of Late Minoan I date and Cretan origin and examines this attribution within the wider discussion of Aegean forgeries. Eliopoulos’s analysis takes the suggested Late Minoan date into account while evaluating whether the ring’s iconography and stylistic features genuinely fit within the Late Minoan artistic repertoire or instead indicate modern manufacture. 

A social-media discussion summarizing popular knowledge about the Ring of Nestor describes it as a roughly 3,700-year-old gold signet ring from Crete, dating to the Late Minoan period (c. 1700–1450 BCE), and states that it is housed in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford. This summary reiterates Evans’s early association with Minoan Crete while aligning the object with a Late Minoan I timeframe and emphasizing ongoing doubts about its authenticity. 

## Archaeological and Historical Context

Evans’s original publication associates the Ring of Nestor with a sepulchral treasure of gold signet rings and bead seals from what he describes as a Mycenaean rock tomb near Thisbë in Boeotia. In this framework, the ring belongs to a burial assemblage characterized by weapons, glass, and pottery that collectively support a late Mycenaean date and a funerary context reflecting elite status. Evans emphasizes the tomb’s role in illuminating aspects of Bronze Age funerary practice and elite material culture. 

In contrast, the online encyclopedia entry places the discovery of the Ring of Nestor before 1907 at Kakovatos in Messenia, linking it to Mycenaean tholos tombs in that region and, in Evans’s view as reported there, to a burial near Pylos. The entry states that Evans argued the ring was made in Minoan Crete during the Late Bronze Age and came from a Mycenaean tholos tomb near Pylos, thus situating the object within the funerary landscape of southwestern Peloponnese rather than Boeotia. 

These differing accounts underscore a conflict in the reported discovery location: Evans’s own description contextualizes the ring within a Mycenaean rock-cut tomb near Thisbë in Boeotia, whereas the later online summary situates it in Kakovatos, Messenia, and connects it to a tomb near Pylos. The available sources do not resolve this discrepancy, and modern iconographic studies such as Eliopoulos’s article focus primarily on stylistic and authenticity questions rather than re-documenting the findspot. 

The broader archaeological setting of Pylos is presented in modern scholarship as the center of a Mycenaean kingdom traditionally associated with the Homeric figure Nestor. Exhibitions such as "Pylos of Nestor. A Mycenaean Kingdom Revealed" trace the development from local centers of power to the palace at Ano Englianos, where the kingdom "traditionally associated with the Homeric Nestor" took shape, emphasizing burial monuments with impressive grave goods as evidence of elite display and social hierarchy. 

Archaeological syntheses describe the palace at Ano Englianos—often called the "Palace of Nestor"—as comprising four main units (Main Building, Southwest Building, Workshop, and Wine Magazine) built with stone rubble walls, ashlar facades, mudbrick upper structures, wooden elements, plastered walls, and concrete floors. Excavations beginning in 1939 and major campaigns under Carl Blegen between 1952 and 1964 revealed that a Middle Helladic town on the hill was cleared to make way for a Late Helladic IIIA palace, with most surviving architecture dated to Late Helladic IIIB. 

The palace at Pylos lacks the massive cyclopean fortifications seen at Mycenae and Tiryns, though a gateway at the northeast end of the hill and wall fragments indicate some degree of fortification. This architectural context frames the environment in which Mycenaean elites, possibly including those associated with elaborate signet rings, operated, providing a backdrop for understanding high-status artifacts linked to Pylian funerary and administrative practices. 

The exhibition on Pylos highlights interconnections between Messenia and the Minoan world, the wider Mycenaean sphere, and the Eastern Mediterranean. It showcases gold and bronze grave goods from tholos tombs at Myrsinochori and Peristeria and a gold-capped agate seal stone with a combat scene from the Grave of the Griffin Warrior near Pylos, demonstrating how funerary assemblages with precious metal rings and seal stones reflect cross-cultural contacts and elite identities. 

Within this broader context, the Griffin Warrior shaft grave near the Palace of Nestor yielded four gold signet rings decorated with Minoan ritual scenes, as well as a finely engraved agate sealstone. These finds have been used to illustrate how Mycenaean elites appropriated and displayed Minoan religious iconography, suggesting that gold signet rings in Pylian burials could function as markers of authority and as vehicles for imported or hybrid religious symbolism. 

## Artistic Features and Iconography

Evans’s 1925 discussion emphasizes the Ring of Nestor as a finely made gold signet ring with a complex figural composition engraved on its bezel. He interprets the imagery as providing a glimpse into a "Minoan after-world" and as reflecting religious conceptions concerning the afterlife and the underworld, which he compares with ancient Egyptian beliefs. The ring is described as part of a "royal treasure" whose craftsmanship and elaborate iconography underscore its association with high-ranking individuals. 

The online encyclopedia summarizes the ring’s imagery as featuring human figures along with both real and fantastical animals and notes that these have been read as depicting scenes from Minoan religion, specifically an underworld or afterlife setting. The entry also reports that Evans saw connections between the ring’s iconography and Egyptian religious imagery, highlighting comparative approaches that situate the ring within wider eastern Mediterranean iconographic traditions. 

Theodore Eliopoulos’s article offers a detailed iconographic analysis of the engraved scene on the Ring of Nestor, examining the figures, their attributes, and the setting to assess possible narrative or ritual meaning. Eliopoulos situates the ring’s imagery within Minoan and Mycenaean religious and artistic traditions, comparing its human and animal figures to Aegean glyptic art in order to evaluate whether the composition fits Late Minoan styles or appears as a modern pastiche. 

Eliopoulos re-examines earlier interpretations, including Evans’s view of the ring as depicting Minoan religious iconography, in light of modern debates about Aegean forgeries. By scrutinizing iconographic details and stylistic parallels, the study considers whether certain features might reflect knowledge of Minoan art available in the early twentieth century rather than genuine Bronze Age artistic conventions, thereby using iconography as a tool for assessing authenticity. 

A social-media discussion summarizing the ring’s features describes the Ring of Nestor as a Late Minoan gold signet ring from Crete whose engraved imagery was interpreted by Evans as depicting religious scenes possibly associated with the underworld. The post further reports that Evans suggested links between Minoan civilization and ancient Egypt based on the ring’s iconography, aligning this interpretation with broader comparative studies of Aegean and Egyptian religious art. 

Comparative work on Aegean signet rings, such as studies of the Isopata Ring, highlights the methodological difficulty of inferring complete myth narratives from Minoan figural compositions. One article critiques earlier readings of the Isopata Ring scene as a detailed narrative of a goddess’s epiphany and instead stresses that complex arrangements of female figures, gestures, and settings on Minoan rings cannot be straightforwardly translated into specific mythological stories. This cautionary approach informs modern evaluations of the Ring of Nestor’s imagery, encouraging restraint in constructing elaborate narratives from its figural program. 

The same Isopata Ring study contrasts Minoan signet rings, which often bear complex figural scenes, with Egyptian signet rings that typically feature oval bezels engraved with hieroglyphs and may be unwieldy as finger rings. This comparison underscores differences in glyptic traditions and suggests that Minoan rings like the Ring of Nestor belong to an Aegean practice of using small, portable objects to carry intricate visual compositions rich in religious or symbolic meaning, rather than functioning primarily as practical sealing devices. 

## Scholarly Debates and Significance

From Evans’s perspective, the Ring of Nestor was significant as an insight into Minoan conceptions of the afterlife and the underworld, offering what he termed a glimpse into the "Minoan after-world". He viewed the ring as a key piece of evidence for reconstructing Bronze Age religious beliefs and for comparing Minoan and Egyptian conceptions of the afterlife, thus granting it considerable interpretive weight in early twentieth-century scholarship on Aegean religion. 

Later discussions, including the online encyclopedia entry, highlight that the ring’s cultural attribution to Minoan Crete and its suggested Late Minoan I date are disputed. The entry notes that some modern scholars regard the ring as a possible modern forgery, while others argue for its authenticity using evidence such as wear patterns, microscopic examination, and iconographic comparison. This debate frames the Ring of Nestor as a contested artifact whose significance for understanding Bronze Age religion and art depends on its status as either genuine or forged. 

Eliopoulos’s 2013 article situates the Ring of Nestor explicitly within the context of Aegean forgeries and authenticity debates. The study compares the ring’s human and animal figures to Minoan and Mycenaean seal imagery to judge whether its iconography matches Late Minoan art or suggests a modern pastiche. Eliopoulos considers a proposed Late Minoan I date and Cretan origin but also entertains the possibility that the ring is a modern creation linked to early twentieth-century Aegean restorers such as Émile Gilliéron. 

A social-media discussion echoes these scholarly concerns, reporting that some scholars suspect the Ring of Nestor may be a modern forgery potentially connected with Émile Gilliéron fils, an art restorer and suspected forger who collaborated with Evans. Other participants in the discussion argue for the ring’s authenticity based on wear patterns, technical and metalworking analysis, and stylistic similarities with genuine Minoan art, while also noting suspicious aspects of the ring’s discovery story. This illustrates the range of opinion on the ring’s status and underscores that its significance is debated. 

Beyond authenticity, broader studies of Aegean signet rings use objects like the Ring of Nestor and the Griffin Warrior rings to explore how engraved rings functioned as technologies of personal authority in the Bronze Age. Analyses of the Griffin Warrior grave describe four gold signet rings engraved with Minoan ritual scenes and emphasize that their ritual imagery and fine craftsmanship conveyed religious symbolism and social status, with the rings intended to carry a man’s mark long after his death. This framework suggests that, if genuine, the Ring of Nestor would have participated in similar practices of encoding identity and authority into portable, high-status artifacts. 

One commenter in the social-media discussion explicitly suggests that, if authentic, the Ring of Nestor most likely functioned as an official seal ring used to authenticate documents, consistent with broader practices of using signet rings as markers of authority. While this is a modern inference rather than a direct ancient testimony, it aligns with scholarship that interprets Aegean signet rings as combining practical sealing functions with the display of religious and social symbolism. 

Comparative iconographic studies, such as the critique of narrative reconstructions on the Isopata Ring, have influenced scholarly treatment of the Ring of Nestor by cautioning against building detailed mythological narratives from glyptic scenes. By emphasizing the limits of iconographic evidence and the risk of over-interpretation, such work encourages a more restrained and methodologically rigorous assessment of what the Ring of Nestor can reveal about Bronze Age religious ideas, even if it is accepted as authentic. 

## Provenance, Subsequent History, and Museum Curation

Evans’s 1925 publication treats the Ring of Nestor and its associated gold signet rings and bead seals as a sepulchral treasure from a Mycenaean rock tomb near Thisbë in Boeotia. In this account, the ring’s early provenance is tied to this burial context and to Evans’s broader interest in linking Mycenaean tomb assemblages with Minoan religious imagery, although the details of acquisition and transfer to his collection are not specified in the summarized sources. 

The online encyclopedia reports that the Ring of Nestor was discovered before 1907 at Kakovatos in Messenia and later entered the Ashmolean Museum’s collection. According to this source, Evans donated the ring to the Ashmolean Museum in 1939, and it is now held there under inventory number AN1938.1130, with the Corpus der Minoischen und Mykenischen Siegel referencing it as CMS VI.229. This establishes a chain of custody from discovery (as reported) through Evans’s possession to its eventual status as a museum object in Oxford. 

The same encyclopedia notes that the ring’s reported findspot and Evans’s role in its collection history have been scrutinized in modern debates about authenticity, with some scholars raising the possibility that restorers such as Émile Gilliéron fils may have been involved in its manufacture. Because the summarized sources do not provide independent archival documentation of the ring’s excavation or acquisition, questions about its provenance remain part of the broader authenticity discussion rather than fully resolved historical facts. 

While detailed exhibition histories of the Ring of Nestor are not outlined in the available sources, broader museum and exhibition narratives concerning Pylos and Mycenaean Messenia provide a relevant curatorial context. The exhibition "Pylos of Nestor. A Mycenaean Kingdom Revealed," organized by the Greek Ministry of Culture and Sports, the Ephorate of Antiquities of Messenia, the J. Paul Getty Museum, and the University of Cincinnati, displays 214 objects from the Archaeological Museum of Messenia and 11 from the National Archaeological Museum to illustrate the development of the kingdom associated with Nestor and its burial monuments with impressive grave goods. 

This traveling exhibition has been shown in Kalamata, at the J. Paul Getty Museum, and at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, highlighting connections between Messenia, the Minoan world, the wider Mycenaean sphere, and the Eastern Mediterranean. Although the Ring of Nestor itself is not explicitly listed among the exhibited objects in the summarized material, the exhibition’s focus on gold rings, seal stones, and other elite grave goods from Pylos-related contexts illustrates how such artifacts are curated as key evidence for Mycenaean kingship, religion, and cross-cultural contacts.

The **Ring of Nestor**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-4) is a gold [signet ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signet_ring "Signet ring") first described by the archaeologist [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") in 1925. According to Evans, it was made on [Minoan Crete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_Crete "Minoan Crete") in the Late Bronze Age and discovered in a [Mycenaean tholos tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") near the ancient site of [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Nestor "Palace of Nestor") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in southwest Greece. The ring has a crowded and complex design, including human figures as well as real and mythical animals, and has been interpreted as indicating aspects of [Minoan religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_religion "Minoan religion"). Evans considered it to show scenes from the [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"), and to illustrate connections between Minoan belief and [ancient Egyptian religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion "Ancient Egyptian religion"). It is currently held by the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), to which Evans gifted it in 1939.

Since its discovery, the ring's authenticity has been debated, with several scholars considering it a modern fake, and others defending it as a genuinely ancient artefact. Arguments in both directions have been made on the grounds of iconographical consistency with other Minoan artworks, and based upon the potential role of [Émile Gilliéron _fils_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Gilli%C3%A9ron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's, in the ring's discovery. Other arguments for authenticity include the wear evident upon the ring and microscopic analysis of its engraving technique, while circumstantial evidence against it has been adduced from Evans's convoluted story of its origins and the fortuitous connections between its iconography and Evans's own ideas about the links between Minoan and Egyptian religion. The ring was removed from display at the Ashmolean in the 20th century, but returned to public view in 1995.

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor is disputed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) Scholars who consider the ring to be ancient date it to the [Late Minoan I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Minoan "Late Minoan") period (c.1700– c.1450 BCE), during the [Neopalatial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neopalatial_Period "Neopalatial Period") of Minoan civilization.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) The ring is made of gold of 97% purity,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020223-6) with the remaining 3% being made up of copper,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) and weighs 31.76 grams (1.12 oz).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159Hughes-BrockBoardman2018448-7) It has a hollow [bezel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bezel "Bezel"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) made of a gold sheet 0.25 mm (0.01 in) in thickness,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8) with a groove for a finger set into the underside. The ring's hoop is decorated with a central band of [embossed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embossing_(manufacturing) "Embossing (manufacturing)") hemispherical pieces,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) which are [soldered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldering "Soldering") onto the hoop,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19989-9) and with [granules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granulation_(jewellery) "Granulation (jewellery)") of two different sizes. These pieces and granules have been deformed, with the most damage apparent on the central band of large hemispheres.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

The hoop is slightly elliptical, with internal diameters of 1.4 and 1.56 cm (0.551 and 0.614 in), a width of 0.82 cm (0.32 in), and a thickness of 0.35 cm (0.14 in). The bezel is 3.29 cm (1.295 in) horizontally and 2.18 cm (0.858 in) vertically.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) Owing to the narrow diameter of the hoop, [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") (who first introduced the ring to scholarship) considered that it was probably intended to be hung on a string rather than worn on the finger.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930146-10)

The iconography on the ring's bezel is divided into four scenes, each occupying a quarter of the face. The scenes are separated by a thicker vertical band and a thinner horizontal band; the vertical band rises out of a base. At the intersection of the vertical band and the base is an animal form, whose identification has been debated. The bands are generally taken to represent the trunk and branches of a large tree.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927549%E2%80%93550-11) The bands were probably made with a [punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_(tool) "Punch (tool)"), while the figures are likely to have been both punched and [engraved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engraving "Engraving").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8)

Of the 99 known signet rings from the Aegean Bronze Age, the Ring of Nestor shows the greatest number of individual figures: it depicts fourteen human figures and at least five other animals.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12) In the scene in the upper-left quadrant, a lion can be seen lying on a large structure, called a "table" by Helen Hughes-Brock and [John Boardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boardman_(art_historian) "John Boardman (art historian)"), beneath which are two naked human women, each with one hand on the table. Four small branches, resembling [ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy "Ivy"), sprout from the vertical dividing-band to the image's right. Below this scene, several women in long, layered skirts can be seen: one walks towards the central band, while two approach a small table on which a [griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin "Griffin") is seated. The women may have the heads of birds, or alternatively simply have their heads leant forwards. Behind the griffin, a female figure stands in a skirt slightly longer than those of the others, facing the ring's centre. Hughes-Brock and Boardman describe these two scenes as "otherworldly", in contrast to the scenes on the ring's right, which only contain human figures.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448%E2%80%93449-13)

[![Image 6: Ancient wall painting: male figure, bare chested and wearing a kilt, carries a jug to the right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg/120px-%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:'Procession_Fresco'_from_Knossos,_Neopalacial_period,_1600_-_1450_BC,_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg)

[![Image 7: Ancient wall-painting: a woman, skin rendered in white, stoops to gather flowers: her hair is elaborately made up and she wears a many-layered skirt](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg/250px-Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cueilleuse_de_safran,_fresque,_Akrotiri,_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg)

Minoan frescoes showing examples of clothing similar to that depicted on the Ring of Nestor

On the right-hand side of the bezel, the upper image shows a pair of women, one sitting and one squatting, facing each other: one may be wearing a skirt, or both may be naked. Next to them are a man and a woman, standing; the man wears a belted [kilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilt "Kilt") and the woman a knee-length layered skirt. Above the human figures can be seen two winged insects and two ovoid shapes identified by Hughes-Brock and Boardman as [pupae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupa "Pupa"). Below this scene is one of four human figures walking towards the centre of the ring: the first and last figures are men, and the two in the middle are women in long, flounced skirts.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448%E2%80%93449-13)

### Interpretation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Interpretation")]

Evans considered the ring to depict scenes from the Minoan [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14) specifically "the admission of the departed into the realms of bliss".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930145-15) He interpreted the shape dividing the four quarters of the ring as "unquestionably a tree, old and gnarled", which he considered to be comparable with the [world tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_tree "World tree") called [Yggdrasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yggdrasil "Yggdrasil") in [Norse mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192550%E2%80%9351-16) He considered the lion to be "the guardian of the [Lower World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld")",[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192514-17) and the creature at the base, which he took to be a dog, to be "the Minoan forerunner of [Cerberus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerberus "Cerberus")"[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14)–the three-headed dog who guards the underworld in classical Greek mythology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOgden2013109-18) The griffin on the bezel is a common motif in Minoan art, originally taken from the Near East.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-19)

Evans wrote in a letter, shortly after seeing the ring, that it depicted "a map of the [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysium "Elysium")" according to the Minoans.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He interpreted the winged insects as butterflies, and as symbols of the [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reincarnation "Reincarnation") of the human beings next to them. In the same scene, he saw the standing female figure as a goddess, and the male figure as a young man reunited with his lover, either after death or possibly upon entering the underworld while alive.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930151%E2%80%93152-20) He considered this goddess to be a [deity of the underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chthonic_deities "Chthonic deities"), the lion (following parallels in Egyptian iconography) to be associated with her, and the two women in the same scene to be her handmaidens.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-21) He described the scene with the griffin as that of souls being tested on entry to "the Halls of the Just in the Griffin's Court", and the griffin itself as a "Chief Inquisitor".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930154-22) Evans characterised the whole scene as "the abode of light rather than of darkness", equivalent to the paradise of Elysium in later Greek mythology.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930155%E2%80%93156-23)[Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos") and Briana Jackson suggest that Evans's interpretation of the scene via Egyptian mythology, as well as his reading of the central motif as a tree, was influenced by James Frazer's _[The Golden Bough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Golden\_Bough "The Golden Bough")_, as well as by the discovery of the [Tomb of Tutankhamun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Tutankhamun "Tomb of Tutankhamun") in 1923.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20119%E2%80%9310-24)

[![Image 8: Grey photograph of the cast of the ring's impression: as infobox image, except the creature at the base of the tree is highly indistinct](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png)

Photograph of a cast of the ring's impression, published by Evans in 1925

[Martin P. Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_P._Nilsson "Martin P. Nilsson") discussed the ring in a 1927 work on Minoan and Mycenaean religion, in which he called it "a most amazing find ... [which] differs most markedly from other Mycenaean rings".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-26)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-27) Nilsson disagreed with Evans's association between the tree motif and the world tree, pointing out that the motif was not known to be attested prior to the eighth century CE; he considered the tree more likely to prefigure the tree in the [Garden of the Hesperides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_the_Hesperides "Garden of the Hesperides") in Greek mythology, which grew golden apples.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927550-28) In support of this, he suggested that the creature labelled by Evans as a proto-Cerberus should be considered a forerunner of [Ladon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladon_(mythology) "Ladon (mythology)"), the dragon who guarded that tree.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927551-29) He considered there to be no compelling reason to suggest that the scenes on the ring were related to the afterlife or the underworld.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927556-30) Galanakis identifies the figure as a dragon, and considers it to be inspired by similar [Babylonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon "Babylon") motifs otherwise rare in Minoan art;[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-31) Hughes-Brock and Boardman call it a "Minoan dragon".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018449-32) Andreas Vlachopoulos identifies it as a scorpion.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12)

[Jean-Claude Poursat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Poursat?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jean-Claude Poursat (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude%20Poursat "fr:Jean-Claude Poursat")], in 1976, suggested that the vertical and horizontal bands represented rivers, a hypothesis initially entertained but dismissed by Evans. In support of this, Poursat argued that the creature at the base was a "fantastical crocodile" or "crocodile-dragon". He further suggested that the lower half of the bezel, assumed to be a single episode by Evans, may have been intended to show two successive scenes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33) Olga Krzyszkowska described Evans's interpretation of the bezel as an underworld scene as "fanciful" in 2005.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 9: Line drawing of a gold ring, in three different orientations](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png)

Line drawing of the ring from the side, published by Evans in 1925[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192547-35)

In 1907, a series of [tholos tombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") at [Kakovatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakovatos "Kakovatos") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in the southwest [Peloponnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnese_(region) "Peloponnese (region)") region of Greece, were excavated by the German archaeologist [Wilhelm Dörpfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_D%C3%B6rpfeld "Wilhelm Dörpfeld").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020224%E2%80%93225-36) According to Evans, the ring was taken by a local peasant from one of these tombs (along with blocks of masonry) prior to the excavation, probably from the grave-pit inside the tomb's chamber.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-39)

In 1924, or possibly earlier, the ring was shown to the acquisitions committee of the [National Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens "National Archaeological Museum, Athens") in Athens, of which the German archaeologist [Georg Karo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Karo "Georg Karo") was a member.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194-40) Following Karo's judgement, the committee rejected the ring as a forgery, created by a modern goldsmith in the early twentieth century.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020226-41) Evans was subsequently informed of the ring's existence by somebody he described as "a trustworthy source" (and later "a friend"): Karo inferred that Evans was referring to [Émile Gilliéron _fils_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Gilli%C3%A9ron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-42) Nanno Marinatos endorsed this view in 2015,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194%E2%80%93195-43) and Vlachopoulos called it "very possible" in 2020.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020225-44)

Evans subsequently travelled to the Peloponnese to view the ring, where he was told that the finder had died, leaving the ring to his son; the son passed it into the possession of the owner of a nearby vineyard.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37) Evans purchased the ring from the vineyard owner between 1924 and 1925,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546Vlachopoulos2020225-45) and named it the "Ring of Nestor" after [the mythological king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") of [the region of Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia_(ancient_region) "Messenia (ancient region)") in the [Homeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer") poems.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He gifted the ring to the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") in 1939.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) It was subsequently removed from display, though placed back there in 1995.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) As of 2018, it remains in the Ashmolean.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

## Debate over authenticity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Debate over authenticity")]

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor has been debated since its introduction to scholarship. In 2019, Angelika Hudler categorised the ring among _gemmae dubitandae_ ('jewels deserving scepticism').[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-48)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) In 2013, Yannis Galanakis called the ring "one of the most controversial Aegean objects in the Ashmolean's collection".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1)

### Arguments against authenticity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Arguments against authenticity")]

Before the 1970s, most scholars considered the ring a forgery.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013210-49) Nilsson, who treated the ring as genuine in 1927, revised the 1950 edition of his work to call it a "suspect object".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20196-50) According to [Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos"), her father [Spyridon Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyridon_Marinatos "Spyridon Marinatos") considered the Ring of Nestor a fake. She cites as evidence a reference in a 1928 letter by Marinatos to "reprimands" Evans was receiving about forgeries.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015190%E2%80%93191-51) Hagen Biesantz argued in 1954 that the ring's iconography was inconsistent with the known corpus of [Minoan art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_art "Minoan art"), and accordingly that the ring was a forgery.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-52)

[![Image 10: A gold ring, like the Ring of Nestor, with an oval bezel inscribed with figures. A youth climbs a hill in the centre to pick something from a tree, while two seated female figures watch.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg/250px-Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg)

The Ring of Minos

Evans published the ring alongside the "Thisbe Treasure" from [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia "Boeotia"), considered a modern forgery, and the connection has cast doubt upon the Ring of Nestor in turn.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34) John Younger, in 1975, suggested that the ring had been forged by Gilliéron _fils_ and [his father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Gilli%C3%A9ron "Émile Gilliéron"), who had also been accused of forging the [Ring of Minos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Minos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ring of Minos (page does not exist)") apparently found at Knossos and also published by Evans.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-53) In 1986,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) the Swedish archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_H%C3%A4gg?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)")[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin%20H%C3%A4gg "sv:Robin Hägg")] separately reported hearing from a collaborator of [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"), who had worked on the Aegean Bronze Age in the 1930s, that Persson had told her that Gilliéron _fils_ had forged the Ring of Nestor: Hägg subsequently heard the same story from the Egyptologist [Torgny Säve-Söderbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torgny_S%C3%A4ve-S%C3%B6derbergh "Torgny Säve-Söderbergh") and from [Doro Levi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doro_Levi "Doro Levi"), director of the [Italian School of Archaeology at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_School_of_Archaeology_at_Athens "Italian School of Archaeology at Athens") from 1947 until 1976.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-54)[Agnes Sakellariou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Sakellariou?action=edit&redlink=1 "Agnes Sakellariou (page does not exist)") upheld the Gilliéron hypothesis in 1994, arguing that the insects labelled as butterflies by Evans had no direct parallels in Minoan art, but could have been based by a forger on Mycenaean examples found in tombs on the Greek mainland.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19983%E2%80%935-55) Krzyszkowska similarly accused the Gilliérons of forging the ring in 2005.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005p._336,_n._113-56)

Nanno Marinatos and Briana Jackson wrote in 2011 that the "complicated chain of transmission" reported to Evans raised suspicion, and made it impossible to verify the truth of the ring's discovery.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20117-57) They also argued that butterflies had no connection to the soul or reincarnation in Minoan culture, but that they were included on the ring because they held this metaphorical function in Victorian thought, and had been incorrectly linked to the concept in Mycenaean culture by [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") and more widely in Frazer's work.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201111%E2%80%9312-58) Marinatos and Jackson suggested that the connections between the ring's design and Egyptian iconography were based directly on _The Golden Bough_, which emphasised the religious role of oak trees and [mistletoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistletoe "Mistletoe"), and calculated to appeal to Evans, who had long sought to establish a relationship between Minoan religion and that of ancient Egypt.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201110-59)

### Arguments in favour of authenticity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ring_of_Nestor&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Arguments in favour of authenticity")]

[V. Gordon Childe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._Gordon_Childe "V. Gordon Childe") wrote in 1925 that "fortunately no such suspicions [of forgery] attach to the unique gold ring", and that it was "undoubtedly a remnant of the regal wealth once buried in the great tombs of Kakovatos".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-62) Yiannis Sakellarakis, in 1973, considered the iconography of the ring to match other known Minoan examples, and so that the ring was likely to be genuine.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-63) Jean-Claude Poursat accepted these arguments in his own publication of 1976.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33)

[![Image 11: Colourful drawing in the style of a Minoan fresco, replicating the bezel of the Ring of Nestor. The creature at the bottom of the tree is rendered as an oddly-posed dog.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png)

Gilliéron's rendering of the ring's impression in the style of a Minoan fresco, published by Evans in 1930

Vlachopoulos suggests that Gilliéron could not have been involved in faking the ring, because his drawing of the bezel for Evans's publications showed a hound for the creature Vlachopoulos identified as a scorpion, demonstrating "his ignorance and his innocence".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12)[Ingo Pini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo_Pini?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ingo Pini (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo%20Pini "de:Ingo Pini")] similarly argued that the different treatment of the creature on the ring and Gilliéron's later painting of the same scene, in which Pini described the rendering as "a rather odd-looking quadruped", indicates that Gilliéron could not have made both.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

Similarly, Theodore Eliopoulos suggested that the "table" on which the lion reclines as a horizontal platform supported by three incurved altars: such a platform was unknown in Minoan iconography at the time of the ring's discovery,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013212%E2%80%93214-65) but later found in the 1970s and 1980s on frescoes from [Akrotiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city) "Akrotiri (prehistoric city)"). Eliopoulos considers this evidence for a genuine Bronze Age origin.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013221-66) Similarly, he argues that the appearance of lions as supporters of goddesses, known from Akrotiri frescoes as well as rings and sealings discovered after 1925, suggest the authenticity of the ring, as the lion's presence was considered anomalous when the ring was first published.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013219-67) Pini argued against Sakellariou's interpretation of the butterflies as without precedent, suggesting that they echoed sealings found at the Cretan site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada"), excavated in 1902–1903 but not published until 1925.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19985-68) He also drew a parallel between the creature at the base of the tree, which he called a "Minoan dragon", and a form on a seal found at [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in the 1990s, while arguing that the motif would not have been known to a forger in the early twentieth century.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

In 1998, [Jack Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ogden_(jewellery_historian) "Jack Ogden (jewellery historian)") studied the manufacturing technique of the ring, and concluded that it matched that of genuine examples, whereby the bezel was carved first, the hoop added, and the back plate of the bezel then soldered into place. In addition, he considered that microscopic analysis of the engraving showed that it had been done according to Mycenaean techniques, which would have been unknown to an early twentieth-century forger.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-69) Ultrasound scans of the ring presented by Walter Müller in 2002 confirmed that it was hollow, dispelling a longstanding belief that it was solid in construction, which would be unusual for a genuinely Bronze Age ring.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM%C3%BCller2003480Krzyszkowska2005p._334,_n._111-70) Pini suggested that the wear on the decorations of the hoop indicates intensive use, and parallels other rings known to be genuine.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini199810-71) Childe similarly suggested that the wear on these parts may suggest that the ring was actually worn, in contrast to Evans's belief.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)

Kate Cooper, in 2021, wrote that the ring was generally considered fake, but that the 2015 discovery of a ring (designated Ring 2) in the [Tomb of the Griffin Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_the_Griffin_Warrior "Tomb of the Griffin Warrior"), a [shaft grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_grave "Shaft grave") at Pylos dating to the [Late Helladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Helladic "Late Helladic") IIA period (c.1400– c.1300 BCE) with similar iconography, particularly the ivy, pointed towards its authenticity.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Nestor#cite_note-72)

## Extract

The first subject of the present communication is a truly royal treasure of gold rings and of bead-seals in the same metal found in a Mycenaean rock tomb near the site of Thisbê in Boeotia. The find was made in 1915, at a time when war conditions diverted the course of discovery from official channels, and a fortunate chain of circumstances now enables me not only to describe but to exhibit to the Society the whole hoard. Under the circumstances it is impossible without a breach of confidence to give all the details, but, from what I have been able to ascertain, the discovery was made by a peasant in a chamber-tomb excavated in the rock, by the village of Dombrena. Near this spot, about a quarter of an hour N.W. of Kakosi, on the Akropolis height of Thisbê, Mr. W. A. Heurtley, of the British School at Athens, kindly informs me that he was shown, in an olive grove, three chamber-tombs with _dromoi_. He adds, ‘The old man who showed me had dug one completely and found a dagger and vases and some sherds, all of which he had lost.’ Mr. Heurtley adds, however, that, from a drawing that the old man made of one of the vases, it is clear that it was a stirrup-vase of late type.

Other objects that I myself was able either to see or secure, found in the same group of tombs, but not authenticated as coming from the chamber containing the treasure, were bronze spear-heads and a short sword with the flange running round the extremity of the hilt, belonging to a very late Mycenaean type. A bronze razor also occurred of an advanced form and, of still later date presumably, a small perforated double-axe head of iron. There were also found a whole set of perforated glass-paste objects with holes below for the attachment of pendant gold disks which Mr. Wace has now conclusively shown to belong to necklaces. The particular type found, as well as certain paste pendants with reliefs covered with gold foil, belongs to the date of the Dimini jewels, or early L.M. III. _b_, in Minoan terms. There is no difficulty in ascribing the radiated glazed clay beads (Fig. 1, _a_) and the bugle bead of _kyanos_ blue paste (Fig. 1, _d_), as well as the plated faience plaques with groups of palms in relief (Fig. 1, _k_), to the same epoch.

page 45 note 4 Unfortunately in the recently published account of the investigations of the British School at Mycenae to which all are indebted for a rich accession of materials, including the most painstaking records and admirable plans (_B.S.A._, xxv.), the term ‘Helladic’—useful enough for the earlier periods—has been extended to include the Mycenaean Age. It starts from the assumption that the earlier phase at Mycenae represents the result not of actual conquest and the abrupt and wholesale displacement of a lower by an incomparably higher form of culture but of a gradual ‘Minoization’ of the native Helladic community. If this, as I believe, untenable position is given up, the whole _raison d'être_ for the term ‘Late Helladic’ ceases to exist. It is a great pity, indeed, that the name Mycenaean, which was already to hand and is generally intelligible, should be thus discarded.

 page 46 note 4b 

page 46 note 4b At the date when Minoan elements first impose themselves on the Peloponnese the predominant type of house belonged to the ‘apsidal’ class. This is seen at Tiryns, Korakou, and elsewhere in the stratum immediately preceding the ‘Mycenaean’ and seems to have been implanted there, in company with cist-graves containing contracted skeletons and bronze implements of peculiar type, by ‘Minyan’ intruders from North of the Gulf. The fixed hearth type of rectangular dwelling is common to both sides of the Aegean and, indeed, to late Neolithic Crete. But so far as the evidence goes, the Mycenaean type of Megaron shows most analogies with the Anatolian. Anyhow, it could not have been evolved _in situ_ from an antecedent type not to be found there in the preceding period.

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

This paper presents an analysis of the iconography surrounding the 'Ring of Nestor' in the context of Aegean forgeries and authenticity debates. By revisiting key iconographic features and comparisons, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the ring's significance in Minoan and Mycenaean art. Observations draw upon historical scholarship and recent discoveries to question and affirm previous conclusions related to the ring's motifs and their implications.

... Read more

## Key takeaways

![Image 11: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

1.   The text explores the authenticity of the 'Ring of Nestor' through iconographic analysis.
2.   Contradictions in technical analysis highlight the importance of iconography in Aegean studies.
3.   The connection between incurved altars and the ring's depiction supports its authenticity.
4.   The ring's iconography may reflect cultural practices from the 1920s.
5.   Generations of scholars have debated the genuineness of both Nestor's and Minos' rings.

## Related papers

[Towards a Consideration of Unprovenanced Ancient and Medieval Finger Rings](https://www.academia.edu/37745254/Towards_a_Consideration_of_Unprovenanced_Ancient_and_Medieval_Finger_Rings)

[TN Pollio](https://independent.academia.edu/TNPollio)

This article will hopefully incentivize researchers to consider examining the untoward thousands of unprovenanced base metal and silver alloy finger rings being uncovered at sites from the U.K to Eurasia. Documented artifacts from controlled and stratified environments are of course essential towards understanding ring typology and routes of transmission across temporal and spatial environments. However, these standard methodologies should not preclude consideration of random and under-documented finds from non-professional sources. The rationale is simply that, within the last several decades, a significant proportion of new finds have in fact been made through amateur channels; and the rings they've uncovered may potentially contribute to our understanding of these underreported artifacts. Within the last few decades, the proliferation of metal detecting and use of the internet have ensured the issue is no longer of availability, but identity. The era of scarcity is obviously over, in view of the burgeoning array of base metal rings encountered on the international market. Any a priori disqualification of such a vast resource of emerging data is to ignore an untapped resource towards our understanding of ancient societies and the material culture associated therewith The need for reliable and broadly accessible reference material becomes increasingly apparent as more and more finger rings are uncovered and presented through on-line and other sources. Types which were once familiar only to academics have suddenly flooded the public conscience; but with little increase in resources towards the understanding of these artifacts. Small finds such as bronze finger rings are routinely uncovered at archaeological sites in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Eurasia. They are typically noted in excavation reports, then cataloged and archived in places such as universities and museums. Unfortunately, both the reports and rings themselves are rarely accessible in mediums available to the general public. In most cases, only other professionals – such as academics and historians – are even aware of their existence. In terms of accessibility, most of this research has been compiled in unfamiliar languages and arcane formats which, to the general public, might as well be written in cuneiform and buried on the dark side of the moon. Many in English speaking countries have some proficiency in languages such as French, German and Spanish. But how many would understand technical reports written in Russian, Polish, Slovak, Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, Hungarian, Turkish or Greek – the languages in which much of this research has been published? Unfamiliar languages and limited/restricted formats are significant impediments toward the dissemination of this otherwise invaluable material.

Tο 2005 παραδόθηκε στο Αρχαιολογικό Μουσείο Θεσσαλονίκης ένα άγνωστης προέλευσης χρυσό δαχτυλίδι με έγγλυφη παράσταση ζευγαρώματος δύο τετράποδων (ΜΘ 23748), το οποίο παρέπεμπε εμφανώς στα κρητομυκηναϊκού τύπου χρυσά σφραγιστικά δαχτυλίδια. Η αναλυτική εξέτασή του έδειξε πως πρόκειται για πλαστό τέχνεργο, κατασκευασμένο στο τέλος του 19ου - αρχή 20ού αιώνα από έναν τεχνίτη με γνώση των δαχτυλιδιών και σφραγιδόλιθων της αιγαιακής Εποχής Χαλκού. Το δαχτυλίδι προσεγγίζεται εδώ ως ένα ιστορικό-πολιτιστικό τεκμήριο. Όχι, όμως, του μακρινού αρχαίου παρελθόντος από το οποίο υποτίθεται πως προέρχεται, αλλά του σύγχρονου κοινωνικού και πολιτιστικού περιβάλλοντος στο οποίο κατασκευάστηκε: ένα αντικείμενο εμπνευσμένο μεν από την αιγαιακή Εποχή Χαλκού, αλλά προορισμένο για σύγχρονη κατανάλωση. Ως τέτοιο ενσωματώνει το τι θεωρούνταν «Μινωικό»/«Μυκηναϊκό» από τον πλαστογράφο του και/ή τους υποψήφιους αγοραστές του, φανερώνοντας παράλληλα τις προκαταλήψεις, ανάγκες και επιθυμίες της εποχής που δημιουργήθηκε. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό επιχειρείται η ιχνηλάτηση των επιλογών του σύγχρονου πλαστογράφου, θέτοντας ερωτήματα, όπως: Πότε κατασκευάστηκε το δαχτυλίδι; Τι ενέπνευσε τον κατασκευαστή του; Ποιες ήταν οι επιλογές του -συνειδητές ή ασυνείδητες- όσον αφορά στο υλικό, την εικονογραφία, την τεχνοτροπία και την τεχνική κατασκευής και διακόσμησης του δαχτυλιδιού; Ποια στοιχεία του δαχτυλιδιού μάς φαίνονται ακόμα και σήμερα «Μινωικά»/«Μυκηναϊκά» και ποια φαντάζουν τελείως «λάθος» και μη πειστικά;

[One Ring to Know Them All: An Experimental Approach to Reconstructing the 'Ring of Hermes'](https://www.academia.edu/122737531/One_Ring_to_Know_Them_All_An_Experimental_Approach_to_Reconstructing_the_Ring_of_Hermes)

[Marios Koutsoukos](https://liverpool.academia.edu/MariosKoutsoukos)

Work In Progress, 2023

In Late Antiquity, no Roman would think twice about questioning the efficacy of ceremonial magic. They might doubt its legitimacy or, perhaps, the methods of the magician, but no one would ever dismiss magic itself as an operative force in the cosmos as well as a direct means of interacting with divine powers. Its potential efficacy was an accepted reality of life for layman and philosopher alike. It is in this cultural milieu that magical formularies such as those preserved in the Greek Magical Papyri circulated amongst ritual experts and Platonic philosophers with an affinity towards theurgy. What was the magical praxis like from the perspective of the operator? How did it enable a direct interaction with divine powers from a lived ancient religions point of view? When addressing these questions, modern scholarship very often confines itself in the traditional approach of textual examination, relying on individual accounts, such as that of the first-century Greek physician Thessalos of Tralles. or second-hand narratives, like those in Porphyry’s Life of Plotinus. The present paper proposes a hybrid method of studying Late Antique magical formularies which combines the methodology of textual approach with that of experimental archaeology. Termed experimental ritualism, this approach is presented through an experiment in reconstructing the magic ‘Ring of Hermes’ (PGM 213-303). This paper uses self-reflection to trace the process from the construction of the physical object itself to its ritual consecration and the attempts at putting the ring to its intended use. In effect, it is not merely the record of an experimental reconstruction but also an attempt at empirically adopting as emic a perspective as possible towards Late Antique magic praxis. Keywords: Graeco-Egyptian Magic; Greek Magical Papyri; Late Antiquity; Experimental Archaeology; Theurgy; Magic Ring.

[Nadine Engels (Becker)](https://lmu-munich.academia.edu/NadineEngelsBecker)

The task of attributing seals to different hands or workshops is still a desideratum in Aegean studies, for the identification of Aegean seal-engravers and goldsmiths and their stylistic output could dramatically change our knowledge of the use, circulation and social impact of certain seals or seal groups and refine our methods of dating this (often only roughly datable) medium. A set of new data and methods now available, such as precise measurements of sizes and weights, x-ray analysis and material analysis finally enable us to shed new light on several questions concerning individual styles and thus to identify " masters " without the usual reliance on iconography. In this article, a set of thirteen signets will be presented in a detailed study highlighting their find contexts, their technical criteria and their iconographical similarities, leading to the conclusion that the rings were very probably made by six different " masters " working in the phases LH II – LH IIIA on Crete and the Greek mainland.

[Yoav Farhi](https://eretzmuseum.academia.edu/YoavFarhi)

Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology

This paper presents a rare bronze finger ring that was found more than half a century ago and bears a symbol known mainly from the coins of Mattathias Antigonus. A teenager recovered it from one of the burial caves in the cliff of Naḥal David at ‘En Gedi. Although the cave was later excavated by Nahman Avigad, the ring was forgotten and was not incorporated in the excavation report. This paper discusses the ring, the symbol it bears, and its relation to the coins of Antigonus. I suggest a date and identification for the burials in the cave that associates them with the conflict between Herod and Antigonus.

What explains the authenticity debate surrounding the ring of Nestor?add

The research highlights that the ring's authenticity was primarily defended by Sakellarakis in 1971 due to iconographic elements like butterflies and griffin-headed women, despite earlier skepticism from many scholars.

How do incurved altars relate to the ring of Nestor's iconography?add

The study proposes that the platform depicted in the ring is supported by incurved altars, mirroring construction styles revealed by the Xeste 3 fresco, unknown to scholars until the 1970s.

When was the ring of Nestor first published and what was its initial reception?add

Published in 1925, the ring was initially viewed with skepticism regarding its authenticity, with many scholars attributing it to a forger's work due to perceived inconsistencies.

How did the research address previous skepticism about the ring of Nestor?add

The paper counters past arguments by demonstrating specific iconographic parallels, such as those identified in the Archanes excavation, revealing a strong cultural connection absent in forgery narratives.

What implications does the ring's iconography have for understanding ancient Aegean culture?add

The findings suggest a rich interplay between religious practices and artistic representations, as seen through elements like the lion, which may represent royal or divine power within ceremonial contexts.

Current Approaches and New Perspectives in Aegean Iconography, Aegis 18 (2020), pp. 223-252.](https://www.academia.edu/43416584/_2020_A_G_Vlachopoulos_The_Ring_of_Nestor_and_the_quest_for_authenticity_in_F_Blakolmer_ed_Current_Approaches_and_New_Perspectives_in_Aegean_Iconography_Aegis_18_2020_pp_223_252)

[Andreas Vlachopoulos](https://lastamp.academia.edu/AndreasVlachopoulos)

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

The Self Possessed: Framing Identity in Late Minoan Glyptic. 17th International Aegean Conference, Venice 17-21 April 2018.](https://www.academia.edu/36262330/Tully_C_J_and_S_Crooks_2018_The_Self_Possessed_Framing_Identity_in_Late_Minoan_Glyptic_17th_International_Aegean_Conference_Venice_17_21_April_2018)

[Sam Crooks](https://independentresearcher.academia.edu/SamCrooks), [Caroline J . Tully](https://unimelb.academia.edu/CarolineTully)

A group of Late Minoan signet rings fashioned in precious metals and engraved with complex and evocative iconographic schemes appears to depict ‘nature’ or ‘rural’ cults enacted at extra-urban sanctuaries, and may have functioned as inalienable possessions implicated in the expression and maintenance of elite identities during the Aegean Bronze Age. The images on the ring bezels depict human figures in association with epiphanic figures situated in settings characterised by the presence of trees and stones, columnar shrines, stepped altars, openwork platforms, tripartite shrines and sanctuary walls, perhaps involving occasional rites and the erection and dismantling of temporary cult structures which can themselves be viewed as architectonic replications of rural cult sites and natural forms. Just as the fabric of these rings and the artistry and technical skill of their production were of restricted accessibility and controlled distribution, we may infer that so, too, the rites, places and activities recorded on these rings were socially restricted. Possession of these distinctive and desirable objects of economic, cultural and symbolic value may have signified access to, involvement in and mastery over such rituals, the special status of the owner delineated and broadcast through the circulating media of clay sealings, advertising their special relationship with forces and places within nature. Over time the personal and cultural memory, knowledge and associations accumulated within these rings may form histories or biographies of the rings themselves, implicating the identities of their past and present owners, and of the wider community. In this way, they can be understood as inalienable possessions, objects invested with authority and authenticity that in turn authenticate the status of their owners. These enduring symbols draw the past into the present, instantiating cultural and cosmological ideals which classify and objectify social relations through referencing the past. Thus these rings function as mnemonic devices, palimpsests of memory, association and affect which store and transmit information about spatially and temporally disbursed places, people and events, memorialising and broadcasting elite association with the (super)natural world and forming part of the material affordances of the world of things which recursively produce, reiterate and transform identities through ecologies of practice: the past mediated in the present through memory materialised in objects.

# Pylos of Nestor. A Mycenaean Kingdom Revealed

## Hellenic National Archaeological Museum, May – October 2026

20 May 2026

by Archaeology Newsroom

*   A
*   A
*   A

*   ![Image 22: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg) ![Image 23: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg) ![Image 24: whatsapp sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/whatsapp.svg) ![Image 25: linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg) ![Image 26: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg) ![Image 27: print sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/print.svg)  

The exhibition “_The Pylos of Nestor. A Mycenaean Kingdom Revealed_” opening on May 26 is presented at the Hellenic National Archaeological Museum as the third station in a journey that began at the Archaeological Museum of Messenia (February–May 2025) and moved on at the J. Paul Getty Museum.

The exhibition has been organized in collaboration with the Ephorate of Antiquities of Messenia, and with the kind contribution of the J. Paul Getty Museum, and the University of Cincinnati (Department of Classics). Each presentation develops in conversation with the former one, and the current version has been reconfigured with a new design concept and enriched narrative approaches.

The temporary exhibition features 214 antiquities from the Ephorate of Antiquities of Messenia and 11 from the Hellenic National Archaeological Museum, engaging in dialogue with selected works from the Museum’s permanent exhibition of the Mycenaean antiquities.

#### The exhibition at a glance

The exhibition’s narrative unfolds as a journey through space and time: from the scattered centers of power to the establishment of the Palace at Ano Englianos, where the kingdom traditionally associated with the Homeric Nestor took shape.

This trajectory is traced through archaeological evidence that reflects the wealth, social organization, and ideological concepts of the time. Burial monuments with impressive grave goods, prestigious objects, and administrative records shed light on the world of local rulers and, ultimately, the emergence of the wanax’s authority. At the same time, the exhibition highlights Messenia’s interconnections with the Minoan world, the wider Mycenaean sphere, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Archaeological research itself also occupies a prominent place. The first excavators of the prehistoric Messenian monuments presented in the exhibition are integrated as an indispensable part of the narrative, underscoring that knowledge of the past is the result of exploration, documentation, and interpretation.

Excerpts from excavation diaries, drawings, and archival photographs are featured throughout the exhibition. Alongside the exhibits, this material provides documentation and brings visitors into contact with less visible aspects of archaeological research and study. These testimonies reveal the process of excavation itself, from the moment of discovery to recording and interpretation.

The final exhibit serves as a reminder of the connection between the heroic Mycenaean era and the centuries that followed. Rather than merely presenting a lost world, the exhibition presents the way through which it is revealed and acquires meaning today.

#### The museographic approach of the exhibition

The exhibition narrative follows the path of a find from its discovery in the excavation field to its analysis within the exhibition’s “laboratory” setting.

Through a system of graphic analysis, diagrams, and comparative information, visitors are invited to observe the data and draw their own conclusions about society and life at the Palace of Nestor during the Bronze Age. In this way, the exhibition transforms the visitor from a passive viewer of archaeological objects into an active investigator of their history.

#### UNIT 1. Petty kingdoms, great wealth (17 th-14th c. BCE)

The long-term and systematic research conducted by foreign Archaeological Schools, the Archaeological Society at Athens and the University of Athens, as well as the Ephorate of Antiquities of Messenia, have demonstrated how, from the 17th to the 14th century BCE, Messenia emerged as a major center of the Mycenaean world, where powerful local principalities developed, sharing common cultural characteristics and a high level of organization. The numerous and richly furnished funerary monuments containing valuable grave goods reflect the prosperity and vitality of a society that interacted with Crete, the Cyclades, and wider networks in the Εastern Mediterranean.

In areas of Messenia such as Myrsinochori, Tragana, Koukounara, Koryphasio, Psari, Nichoria, Daras, and Vlachopoulo, tholos tombs with rich grave goods predominate. In other sites such as Chora (Volimidia), Peristeria, and Antheia, tholos tombs coexist with other types of graves (such as shaft graves and chamber tombs), forming a complex funerary landscape that reflects social hierarchy and perceptions of the afterlife.

The rulers of the time displayed their power and prestige through precious grave offerings and elaborate funerary customs.

#### UNIT 2. Before the Palace. The Rulers of Ano Englianos

From the end of the Middle Helladic and during the early Mycenaean period, a powerful political and economic center emerged at Ano Englianos. This is evidenced by the rich finds of funerary monuments in the area that would later be occupied by the Palace of Nestor.

Multiple tholos tombs have been excavated, along with chamber tombs and two shaft graves, one of which is the Grave of the Griffin Warrior.

#### UNIT 3. The Kingdom of Nestor

_…_ _for thrice, men say, has he been king for a generation of men,_

Homer,_The Odyssey,_ Book 3, 245

Homer,_The Odyssey,_ Translated by A.T. Murray (1919 edition), Cambridge, Massachusetts, London.

In 1939, Carl W. Blegen and Konstantinos Kouroυniotis uncovered one of the most important Mycenaean palaces in mainland Greece during excavations in Messenia. This Palace was identified as the Homeric Pylos of King Nestor. Built shortly after 1300 BCE, it served as the administrative center of a powerful kingdom that controlled almost the entire region of modern-day Messenia.

At the heart of the Palace stood the Throne Room, adorned with rich wall paintings, where the king exercised his authority. The ground floor comprised more than 100 rooms including residential quarters, workshops, and storerooms filled with vases used for official banquets. Near the entrance was the palace archive, where the first Linear B tablets were found in mainland Greece. These accounting texts are a valuable source of information on the administration, economy and social organisation of the Mycenaean state. The Palace was destroyed by a major fire around 1200 BCE and the hill of Ano Englianos was abandoned as were many other sites in Messenia.
